question: The Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI), the first development finance institution set up in the country, was established in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1948.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI) was set up in 1948, under the Industrial Finance Corporation Act, 1948. (भारतीय औद्योगिक वित्त निगम — 1948)

 

• It was the first development finance institution (DFI) in India, established to provide medium and long-term finance to industry at a time when the capital market was too thin to supply it.

 

• It was converted into a public limited company in 1993, and its name changed to IFCI Limited.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The development finance institutions and their years — a set examined constantly:

 

• IFCI – 1948, the first

 

• ICICI – 1955, set up with World Bank participation; converted into a bank in 2002

 

• IDBI – 1964, set up as a subsidiary of the RBI and made the apex DFI

 

• NABARD – 1982, on the recommendation of the Sivaraman Committee

 

• EXIM Bank – 1982; SIDBI – 1990; NHB – 1988

 

• NaBFID – 2021, the newest, for infrastructure financing

 

NOTE

 

• 1955 (Option 2): The year ICICI was established — and also the year the State Bank of India was constituted. A crowded year, and the strongest distractor here.

 

• 1964 (Option 3): The year IDBI was set up, which became the apex development finance institution and took over the coordinating role.

 

• 1982 (Option 4): The year both NABARD and the EXIM Bank were established.

question: Which is the largest gland in the human body?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Liver.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The LIVER is the largest gland in the human body, and also its largest internal organ, weighing about 1.5 kg in an adult. (यकृत — सबसे बड़ी ग्रंथि)

 

• It is an exocrine gland: it secretes bile, which passes through a duct to the small intestine. Bile contains no digestive enzyme; it emulsifies fats, breaking large globules into small droplets so that lipase can act on them.

 

• The liver performs several hundred functions besides. The principal ones are:

 

• Storage of glucose as glycogen, and of vitamins A, D and B12

 

• Detoxification of alcohol, drugs and other poisons

 

• Conversion of ammonia into urea for excretion

 

• Manufacture of plasma proteins and of clotting factors

 

• Destruction of worn-out red blood cells

 

• It is the only human organ capable of regenerating itself after a substantial part has been removed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Glands classified by how they secrete:

 

• Exocrine – secrete through a duct: salivary, sweat, liver, tear glands

 

• Endocrine – secrete directly into the blood, having no duct: pituitary, thyroid, adrenal

 

• Mixed – both: the pancreas, which secretes pancreatic juice through a duct and insulin into the blood

 

• The pituitary is the smallest gland and is called the master gland, since it controls the others.

 

NOTE

 

• Pancreas (Option 1): The second largest gland, and the only mixed gland. It is the strongest distractor, and worth remembering for its dual character rather than its size.

 

• Thyroid (Option 3): The largest endocrine gland, in the neck, secreting thyroxine. Its deficiency causes goitre, and iodine is needed to make its hormone.

 

• Salivary gland (Option 4): Three pairs — parotid, submandibular and sublingual — secreting saliva with the enzyme salivary amylase, which begins the digestion of starch.

question: Which Mahajanapada had its capital at Rajagriha (Rajgir)?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Magadha.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• MAGADHA had its early capital at Rajagriha (Rajgir), in present-day Bihar. (मगध — राजगृह)

 

• It was later shifted to Pataliputra by Udayin, the son of Ajatashatru, and Pataliputra remained the capital through the Nanda, Mauryan and Gupta periods.

 

• Magadha rose to be the most powerful of the sixteen Mahajanapadas, and its advantages were geographical as much as political:

 

• Iron ore deposits nearby, for weapons and tools

 

• Fertile alluvial soil and a good rainfall

 

• The Ganga and its tributaries for trade and for troop movement

 

• Elephants from the eastern forests for the army

 

• Its principal dynasties were the Haryanka (Bimbisara, Ajatashatru), the Shishunaga, the Nanda and the Maurya.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rajagriha is also called Girivraja, "surrounded by hills", being ringed by five of them. The First Buddhist Council was held there, in the Sattapanni cave, immediately after the Buddha's death.

 

• The four great Mahajanapadas that contended for supremacy were Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti — and Magadha absorbed the rest.

 

NOTE

 

• Kosala (Option 2): Capital at Shravasti, with Ayodhya as a second centre. Its king Prasenajit was a contemporary of the Buddha.

 

• Avanti (Option 3): Capital at Ujjain in the north and Mahishmati in the south. Its king was Pradyota.

 

• Vatsa (Option 4): Capital at Kaushambi, near Prayagraj, ruled by Udayana, the hero of several later Sanskrit plays.

question: Which motion, if passed in the Lok Sabha, obliges the entire Council of Ministers to resign?
solution_text:
The correct answer is No-confidence motion.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A NO-CONFIDENCE MOTION may be moved only in the Lok Sabha, and if it is passed the entire Council of Ministers must resign. (अविश्वास प्रस्ताव)

 

• Its basis is Article 75(3), which makes the Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

 

• It requires the support of at least 50 members to be admitted, and no reasons need be stated in it.

 

• The first no-confidence motion was moved by Acharya J.B. Kripalani in 1963, against Nehru's government.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The parliamentary motions compared — and the differences are the whole of this question:

 

• No-confidence motion – Lok Sabha only; needs 50 members; no reasons required; if passed, the whole Council must resign

 

• Censure motion – Lok Sabha only; reasons must be stated; may be against an individual minister or the whole Council; if passed, the government need NOT resign

 

• Adjournment motion – to draw attention to a definite matter of urgent public importance; needs 50 members; involves an element of censure

 

• Calling attention motion – an Indian innovation, by which a member calls a minister's attention to a matter and obtains a statement; it carries no censure

 

• Confidence motion – moved by the government itself to prove its majority

 

NOTE

 

• Adjournment motion (Option 1): Sets aside the ordinary business of the House to discuss an urgent matter. It censures the government but does not unseat it.

 

• Censure motion (Option 2): The strongest distractor, and the distinction most often missed. A censure motion must state its grounds, may be directed at a single minister, and even when passed does not compel resignation.

 

• Calling attention motion (Option 4): Merely obtains a statement from the minister concerned, and carries no element of censure at all.

question: In which year is Emperor Ashoka believed to have died, an event conventionally taken to mark the beginning of the decline of the Mauryan empire?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 232 BCE.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ashoka is believed to have died in about 232 BCE, after a reign of some forty years beginning around 268 BCE. (अशोक की मृत्यु — लगभग 232 ईसा पूर्व)

 

• His death is conventionally taken as the point from which the Mauryan empire began to decline. His successors — Dasharatha, Samprati, Salisuka and others — were unable to hold the empire together, and it broke up within fifty years.

 

• The causes usually given for the decline are the weakness of the later rulers, the size of the empire and the difficulty of administering it, the cost of the bureaucracy, and — on one older view — Ashoka's pacifist policy, though this last is now much disputed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The chronology of the Mauryas:

 

• 322 BCE – Chandragupta Maurya founds the empire with the help of Chanakya (Kautilya)

 

• c. 297 BCE – Bindusara succeeds

 

• c. 268 BCE – Ashoka succeeds

 

• c. 261 BCE – the Kalinga War

 

• c. 232 BCE – death of Ashoka

 

• 185 BCE – the last Mauryan, Brihadratha, is killed by Pushyamitra Shunga

 

NOTE

 

• 261 BCE (Option 1): The year of the Kalinga War, fought in the eighth year of Ashoka's reign and described by him in Major Rock Edict XIII.

 

• 185 BCE (Option 3): The year the Mauryan empire ended, when Brihadratha was assassinated — nearly fifty years after Ashoka's death. This is the strongest distractor, since both dates concern the end of Mauryan power.

 

• 322 BCE (Option 4): The year the empire was founded by Chandragupta Maurya.

question: Pandit Shivkumar Sharma, who brought a folk instrument of Kashmir onto the classical concert stage, was a maestro of which instrument?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Santoor.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Pandit Shivkumar Sharma (1938-2022) was the maestro of the SANTOOR, and it was he who established it as a classical solo instrument. (संतूर — पंडित शिवकुमार शर्मा)

 

• The santoor is a hundred-stringed trapezoidal instrument, struck with a pair of light wooden mallets called mezrab. Its name comes from the Persian *santur*.

 

• Before him it was a folk instrument of Kashmir, used in the Sufiana Mausiqi tradition, and it had never been played as a classical solo instrument. He modified its construction to allow the sustained notes that Hindustani music requires, and gave his first recital in 1955.

 

• With the flautist Hariprasad Chaurasia he composed the music for Silsila, Chandni, Lamhe and Darr, under the joint name "Shiv-Hari".

 

• He received the Padma Shri (1991) and the Padma Vibhushan (2001).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Maestros and their instruments — a set examined constantly:

 

• Santoor – Shivkumar Sharma; Flute (Bansuri) – Hariprasad Chaurasia, Pannalal Ghosh

 

• Sitar – Ravi Shankar, Vilayat Khan, Nikhil Banerjee

 

• Sarod – Ali Akbar Khan, Amjad Ali Khan

 

• Shehnai – Bismillah Khan; Tabla – Zakir Hussain, Alla Rakha

 

• Sarangi – Ram Narayan; Mandolin – U. Srinivas

 

• Violin (Carnatic) – L. Subramaniam; Veena – S. Balachander

 

NOTE

 

• Sarod (Option 1): A fretless plucked instrument with a metal fingerboard and a skin-covered belly, associated with Ali Akbar Khan and Amjad Ali Khan.

 

• Rudra Veena (Option 2): A large plucked instrument of the dhrupad tradition, with two gourd resonators, associated with the Dagar family.

 

• Sarangi (Option 3): A bowed instrument, held upright and stopped with the fingernails, whose tone is held to come closest to the human voice. Pandit Ram Narayan brought it to the solo stage.

question: Who formulated the law stating that, at a constant temperature, the pressure of a given mass of gas is inversely proportional to its volume?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Robert Boyle.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• BOYLE'S LAW, formulated by Robert Boyle in 1662, states that at constant temperature the pressure of a given mass of gas is inversely proportional to its volume. (बॉयल का नियम)

 

• P ∝ 1/V, or PV = constant, so that P₁V₁ = P₂V₂

 

• In plain terms: squeeze a gas into half the space and its pressure doubles.

 

• The law explains why a balloon expands as it rises — the pressure outside falls, so the volume increases — and why bubbles from a diver grow larger as they approach the surface.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The gas laws, and what each holds constant:

 

• Boyle's law – constant temperature; P ∝ 1/V

 

• Charles's law – constant pressure; V ∝ T

 

• Gay-Lussac's law – constant volume; P ∝ T

 

• Avogadro's law – equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules

 

• Combining them gives the ideal gas equation, PV = nRT.

 

NOTE

 

• Jacques Charles (Option 1): Gave Charles's law, that at constant pressure the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature. He was also a balloonist, which is how he came to study the behaviour of gases.

 

• Amedeo Avogadro (Option 3): Gave Avogadro's law, and the constant 6.022 × 10²³ — the number of particles in one mole — is named after him.

 

• John Dalton (Option 4): Gave the atomic theory and the law of partial pressures, that the total pressure of a mixture of gases equals the sum of the pressures each would exert alone.

question: The Satyashodhak Samaj, founded in 1873 to oppose caste discrimination and priestly domination, was established by _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jyotiba Phule.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Satyashodhak Samaj — the "Society of Truth Seekers" — was founded at Pune on 24 September 1873 by Jyotiba Phule. (सत्यशोधक समाज — ज्योतिबा फुले)

 

• Its object was to free the lower castes from the domination of the Brahmins, and to make education available to those long denied it.

 

• It taught that no priest was needed to perform a marriage or a religious rite, and it conducted ceremonies without priests and without expense.

 

• Phule and his wife Savitribai Phule had earlier opened, in 1848, the first school for girls in Pune — she is regarded as the first woman teacher of modern India.

 

• He wrote "Gulamgiri" (Slavery, 1873) and "Shetkaryacha Asud" (The Cultivator's Whipcord), and it was he who gave currency to the term "Dalit".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Reform movements and their founders — a set frequently examined:

 

• Brahmo Samaj (1828) – Raja Ram Mohan Roy

 

• Prarthana Samaj (1867) – Atmaram Pandurang, with Ranade and Bhandarkar

 

• Arya Samaj (1875) – Dayanand Saraswati

 

• Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) – Jyotiba Phule

 

• Ramakrishna Mission (1897) – Swami Vivekananda

 

• Servants of India Society (1905) – Gopal Krishna Gokhale

 

• Self-Respect Movement (1925) – E.V. Ramasamy Periyar

 

NOTE

 

• Gopal Ganesh Agarkar (Option 2): A social reformer of the same generation and the first editor of Kesari, who broke with Tilak over the priority of social reform against political agitation.

 

• M.G. Ranade (Option 3): A founder of the Prarthana Samaj and of the Widow Remarriage Association, and a pioneer of Indian economic thought.

 

• D.K. Karve (Option 4): A reformer devoted to the cause of widow remarriage and women's education, who founded the first women's university in India in 1916 — now SNDT. He received the Bharat Ratna in 1958.

question: Which of the following languages was granted classical language status in 2024, together with Marathi, Pali, Prakrit and Assamese?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bengali.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• BENGALI was granted classical language status in October 2024, in a single decision that also covered Marathi, Pali, Prakrit and Assamese. (बांग्ला — शास्त्रीय भाषा, 2024)

 

• That decision took the number of classical languages in India from six to eleven.

 

• The eleven, with the years in which each was recognised:

 

• Tamil – 2004 (the first); Sanskrit – 2005

 

• Kannada and Telugu – 2008

 

• Malayalam – 2013; Odia – 2014

 

• Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali – 2024

 

• The criteria are high antiquity of early texts over 1,500 to 2,000 years, a body of ancient literature regarded as a heritage, an original literary tradition not borrowed from elsewhere, and the possibility that the classical form may be distinct from the modern one.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Classical status must not be confused with the Eighth Schedule, which lists 22 scheduled languages for official purposes. Pali and Prakrit are classical but are not in the Eighth Schedule; Hindi is in the Eighth Schedule but is not classical, since it fails the test of antiquity.

 

• A classical language receives central support for its study — international awards for scholars, a Centre of Excellence, and professorial chairs in universities.

 

NOTE

 

• Odia (Option 1): Recognised in 2014, ten years earlier, and the first language from eastern India to receive the status. It is the strongest distractor for that reason.

 

• Malayalam (Option 2): Recognised in 2013.

 

• Telugu (Option 4): Recognised in 2008, together with Kannada.

question: The Champaran Satyagraha of 1917, Mahatma Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, concerned the forced cultivation of which crop?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Indigo.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Champaran Satyagraha (1917) was directed against the forced cultivation of INDIGO in the Champaran district of Bihar. (चंपारण सत्याग्रह — नील की खेती)

 

• Under the "Tinkathia" system, a tenant was obliged to plant three kathas out of every twenty of his holding with indigo for the European planter, whatever the price and whatever his own needs.

 

• The system had become ruinous after synthetic dyes were developed in Germany and the price of natural indigo collapsed — the planters then demanded compensation from the peasants for releasing them from the obligation.

 

• Gandhi was invited to Champaran by Raj Kumar Shukla, a local cultivator who followed him persistently until he agreed to come.

 

• The government appointed an enquiry committee with Gandhi as a member, and the Tinkathia system was abolished; the planters refunded a part of the illegal exactions.

 

• It was Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, and among those who joined him were Rajendra Prasad, Brajkishore Prasad, J.B. Kripalani and Mahadev Desai.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gandhi's three early campaigns, in order:

 

• Champaran, 1917 – indigo cultivators of Bihar

 

• Ahmedabad Mill Strike, 1918 – textile workers; Gandhi's first hunger strike

 

• Kheda, 1918 – peasants of Gujarat seeking remission of revenue after a failed harvest; Gandhi's first non-cooperation

 

NOTE

 

• Cotton (Option 1): The crop of the Ahmedabad mills, where Gandhi's 1918 campaign was on behalf of the workers rather than the growers.

 

• Sugarcane (Option 3): Not the subject of any of Gandhi's early campaigns.

 

• Jute (Option 4): The crop of Bengal, and the subject of much agrarian distress — but not of Champaran.

question: In which year was the first complete and synchronous census of India conducted?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1881.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first complete and synchronous census of India was conducted in 1881, under Lord Ripon, and was supervised by W.C. Plowden, the first Census Commissioner of India. (1881 — प्रथम पूर्ण एवं समकालिक जनगणना)

 

• Synchronous means that the count was taken everywhere on the same night, so that nobody could be counted twice and nobody missed.

 

• An earlier count had been made in 1872 under Lord Mayo, but it was not synchronous — different provinces were enumerated at different times, and some areas were left out altogether. It is therefore called the first census, but not the first complete one.

 

• Since 1881 the census has been taken every ten years without a break, and the Census of 2011 was the 15th in the series and the 7th after independence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Landmark years in Indian census history:

 

• 1872 – first census, under Lord Mayo; non-synchronous

 

• 1881 – first complete and synchronous census, under Lord Ripon

 

• 1921 – the "Great Divide": the only decade in which India's population fell, because of the influenza epidemic of 1918 and famine

 

• 1951 – the "Year of the Great Divide" in the demographic sense, after which growth accelerated sharply

 

• The census is conducted under the Census Act, 1948, by the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India, who works under the Ministry of Home Affairs. The census is a Union subject, listed at entry 69 of the Union List.

 

NOTE

 

• 1872 (Option 1): The year of the first census, under Lord Mayo — but it was taken at different times in different provinces and did not cover the whole country. This is the strongest distractor, and the distinction between *first* and *first complete* is the whole point of the question.

 

• 1901 (Option 3): An ordinary decennial census, notable only for being the first of the twentieth century.

 

• 1921 (Option 4): The "Great Divide" — the one census in which the population of India was recorded as having declined.

question: Coulomb's law states that the electrostatic force between two point charges is inversely proportional to _____.
option_2: the cube of the distance between them
option_3: the square of the distance between them
option_4: the sum of the two charges
solution_text:
The correct answer is the square of the distance between them.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• COULOMB'S LAW, given by Charles-Augustin de Coulomb in 1785, states that the electrostatic force between two point charges is:

 

• directly proportional to the product of the two charges, and

 

• inversely proportional to the SQUARE of the distance between them

 

• F = k q₁q₂ / r², where k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² in free space

 

• The consequence of the inverse-square relation is worth fixing: doubling the distance reduces the force to a quarter, and trebling it to a ninth.

 

• The force acts along the line joining the two charges, and is repulsive between like charges and attractive between unlike charges.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Coulomb's law has the same mathematical form as Newton's law of gravitation, F = G m₁m₂/r² — both are inverse-square laws. The differences are that gravitation is always attractive and enormously weaker, whereas the electrostatic force may attract or repel.

 

• Coulomb's law holds only for point charges at rest, and the value of k depends on the medium: in a medium of dielectric constant K, the force is reduced K times.

 

• The SI unit of charge, the coulomb, is named after him.

 

NOTE

 

• the distance between them (Option 1): Would make the force fall off far too slowly — halving at double the distance rather than falling to a quarter.

 

• the cube of the distance (Option 2): No fundamental force of nature follows an inverse-cube law of this kind. The relation between two dipoles approximates it, but that is a different case.

 

• the sum of the two charges (Option 4): Wrong twice over — the force depends on the product of the charges, not their sum, and that relation is direct, not inverse.

question: The disease "osteoporosis" principally affects which system of the human body?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The skeletal system.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• OSTEOPOROSIS affects the SKELETAL SYSTEM. The word itself says so: Greek osteon ("bone") + poros ("pore") — literally *porous bone*. (ऑस्टियोपोरोसिस — अस्थि तंत्र)

 

• In this condition the bone loses density and becomes brittle, so that a fracture may follow a fall, or even a cough, that would not have injured a healthy bone. The wrist, the hip and the spine are the commonest sites.

 

• It is called a "silent disease", because there are no symptoms at all until a bone breaks.

 

• Its principal causes are a deficiency of calcium and vitamin D, the fall in oestrogen after menopause — which is why women are far more often affected — and advancing age.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Diseases of bone worth distinguishing:

 

• Osteoporosis – loss of bone density; brittle bones

 

• Osteomalacia – softening of the bones in adults, from vitamin D deficiency

 

• Rickets – the same deficiency in children, producing bowed legs

 

• Arthritis – inflammation of the joints, not of the bone itself

 

• Osteoarthritis – wearing away of the cartilage in the joints

 

• The human body has 206 bones in the adult and about 300 at birth, many of which fuse as the child grows. The femur is the longest bone and the stapes in the ear the smallest.

 

NOTE

 

• The nervous system (Option 1): Affected by Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, epilepsy and multiple sclerosis.

 

• The respiratory system (Option 3): Affected by asthma, tuberculosis, bronchitis, pneumonia and silicosis.

 

• The circulatory system (Option 4): Affected by hypertension, atherosclerosis, anaemia and thrombosis.

question: Regular television broadcasting in India began, on an experimental basis in Delhi, in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1959.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Television broadcasting in India began on 15 September 1959, on an experimental basis in Delhi, with the help of UNESCO and equipment presented by Philips. (भारत में टेलीविजन — 1959)

 

• The service transmitted for one hour, twice a week, and its purpose was educational — programmes on health, citizenship and community development for a few dozen teleclubs.

 

• Daily transmission began only in 1965, and television reached Bombay in 1972.

 

• Doordarshan was separated from All India Radio as an independent organisation on 1 April 1976.

 

• Colour television was introduced in 1982, for the Asian Games held in Delhi.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Landmarks in Indian broadcasting:

 

• 1923 – radio broadcasting begins with the Radio Club of Bombay

 

• 1927 – the Indian Broadcasting Company; 1936 – renamed All India Radio

 

• 1957 – Akashvani adopted as the name of AIR; Vividh Bharati launched

 

• 1959 – television begins in Delhi

 

• 1976 – Doordarshan separated from AIR

 

• 1997 – Prasar Bharati established as an autonomous corporation

 

NOTE

 

• 1947 (Option 1): The year of independence. No television service existed anywhere in India.

 

• 1965 (Option 3): The year daily transmission began, and news bulletins were introduced. It is the strongest distractor, since it marks the beginning of regular service rather than of broadcasting itself.

 

• 1976 (Option 4): The year Doordarshan was constituted as a separate organisation, seventeen years after the first transmission.

question: Who is the author of the play "Tughlaq"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Girish Karnad.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Tughlaq" (1964) was written by Girish Karnad, in Kannada, and later translated by him into English. (तुगलक — गिरीश कर्नाड)

 

• It takes as its subject Muhammad bin Tughlaq, the Sultan of Delhi whose reign combined remarkable intelligence with a series of ruinous decisions — the transfer of the capital to Daulatabad, and the token currency.

 

• The play was widely read as a commentary on the India of the 1960s: an idealistic beginning followed by disillusionment, which is why it was so much discussed at the time.

 

• Karnad's other plays include "Yayati", "Hayavadana", "Nagamandala" and "Tale-Danda". He received the Jnanpith Award in 1998 and the Padma Bhushan in 1992.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The four writers who created modern Indian theatre in the 1960s, each in a different language:

 

• Girish Karnad – Kannada; *Tughlaq*, *Hayavadana*, *Nagamandala*

 

• Vijay Tendulkar – Marathi; *Ghashiram Kotwal*, *Silence! The Court is in Session*, *Sakharam Binder*

 

• Mohan Rakesh – Hindi; *Ashadh Ka Ek Din*, *Adhe Adhure*, *Lehron Ke Rajhans*

 

• Badal Sircar – Bengali; *Evam Indrajit*, *Bhoma*, and the founder of the Third Theatre movement

 

NOTE

 

• Vijay Tendulkar (Option 2): Wrote in Marathi, and his *Ghashiram Kotwal* is also a historical play about power and its corruptions — which makes him the closest distractor here.

 

• Mohan Rakesh (Option 3): Wrote in Hindi, and his *Ashadh Ka Ek Din* is built around the poet Kalidasa. He was also a leading figure of the Nayi Kahani movement.

 

• Badal Sircar (Option 4): Wrote in Bengali and took theatre out of the auditorium into open spaces, founding what he called the Third Theatre.

question: Who is the author of "Indica: A Deep Natural History of the Indian Subcontinent"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pranay Lal.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Indica: A Deep Natural History of the Indian Subcontinent" (2016) was written by Pranay Lal, a biochemist by training. (इंडिका — प्रणय लाल)

 

• It is a natural history of the subcontinent, tracing its story from the formation of the earth through the breaking away of the Indian plate from Gondwana, its long journey north, its collision with Asia and the raising of the Himalaya, to the Deccan Traps and the arrival of the earliest human beings.

 

• Its subject is therefore the physical and biological past of India rather than its political past, which is unusual in Indian writing.

 

• His later book, "Invisible Empire: The Natural History of Viruses" (2021), was published during the pandemic.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Books on India by contemporary writers, worth distinguishing:

 

• "India After Gandhi" and "Gandhi Before India" – Ramachandra Guha

 

• "The Idea of India" – Sunil Khilnani; also *Incarnations: India in 50 Lives*

 

• "An Era of Darkness" and "The Great Indian Novel" – Shashi Tharoor

 

• "Indica" – Pranay Lal

 

• "Early Indians" – Tony Joseph, on the peopling of the subcontinent

 

• "The Discovery of India" – Jawaharlal Nehru, written in Ahmednagar Fort prison

 

NOTE

 

• Ramachandra Guha (Option 1): A historian of modern India and of cricket, author of "India After Gandhi", "A Corner of a Foreign Field" and the two-volume life of Gandhi. His subject is political and social history, not natural history.

 

• Sunil Khilnani (Option 3): Author of "The Idea of India" (1997), a study of the making of the Indian republic.

 

• Shashi Tharoor (Option 4): Author of "An Era of Darkness", on the economic consequences of British rule, and of "The Great Indian Novel", which retells the Mahabharata as the story of the freedom movement.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?

I. The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act was enacted in 2003.
II. Under the FRBM Act, the Government of India is required to eliminate the fiscal deficit entirely.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement I is CORRECT. The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act was enacted in 2003 and came into force in July 2004. (एफआरबीएम अधिनियम — 2003)

 

• Statement II is INCORRECT. The Act has never required the fiscal deficit to be eliminated. What it prescribed was:

 

• The elimination of the REVENUE deficit, and

 

• The reduction of the FISCAL deficit to 3% of GDP

 

• The distinction between the two deficits is the whole point of the question:

 

• Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts. It represents borrowing to meet day-to-day expenditure, and is the more serious of the two.

 

• Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − total receipts excluding borrowings. Some fiscal deficit is regarded as legitimate, since it may finance capital expenditure that creates assets.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The N.K. Singh Committee (2017) reviewed the Act and recommended a debt-to-GDP ratio of 60% as the primary anchor — 40% for the Centre and 20% for the States — with a fiscal deficit of 2.5% by 2023.

 

• The Act contains an escape clause, allowing the targets to be relaxed in circumstances such as national calamity, war, or a collapse of agricultural output. It was invoked during the COVID-19 pandemic, when the fiscal deficit rose above 9% of GDP.

 

NOTE

 

• Since Statement I is correct and Statement II is not, Option 2 (Only II), Option 3 (Both I and II) and Option 4 (Neither I nor II) are all ruled out.

 

• Statement II is made false by a single word — "entirely". The Act sets a ceiling on the fiscal deficit; only the revenue deficit was to be eliminated.

question: In cricket, a batter is given out "_____" when he dislodges the bails with his own bat or body while playing a shot or setting off for a run.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Hit Wicket.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A batter is out HIT WICKET when he dislodges the bails with his own bat, person or equipment while playing a shot or in setting off for the first run. (हिट विकेट)

 

• The dismissal is governed by Law 35 of the Laws of Cricket.

 

• The essential point is that the batter himself breaks the wicket — not the bowler, not a fielder. A cap or a helmet falling onto the stumps counts, and so does the bat slipping from the hands.

 

• He is not out hit wicket if the wicket is broken while he is avoiding a run out, or after he has completed his stroke and set off, or in avoiding a throw.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The ways of being dismissed in cricket:

 

• Bowled – the delivery breaks the wicket

 

• Caught – the ball is caught before touching the ground

 

• Leg Before Wicket (LBW) – the ball would have hit the stumps but for the batter's body

 

• Run out – the wicket is broken by a fielder while the batter is out of his ground

 

• Stumped – the wicketkeeper breaks the wicket while the batter is out of his ground and not attempting a run

 

• Hit wicket, Obstructing the field, Hit the ball twice, Timed out, and Retired out

 

• Caught is by far the commonest dismissal; Timed out the rarest — it occurred in a men's international for the first time in 2023.

 

NOTE

 

• Bowled (Option 1): The delivery itself breaks the wicket. The distinction from hit wicket is simply what strikes the stumps — the ball, or the batter.

 

• Stumped (Option 3): The wicketkeeper breaks the wicket while the batter has stepped out of his crease and is not attempting a run. The closest distractor, since both involve a batter out of position.

 

• Run out (Option 4): A fielder or the keeper breaks the wicket while the batter is short of his ground attempting a run.

question: The Gwalior Fort, which Babur described as "the pearl among the fortresses of Hind", is located in which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Madhya Pradesh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Gwalior Fort stands on a sandstone hill above the city of Gwalior, in MADHYA PRADESH. (ग्वालियर किला — मध्य प्रदेश)

 

• Babur described it in the *Baburnama* as "the pearl among the fortresses of Hind".

 

• Its most celebrated building is the Man Mandir Palace, built by Raja Man Singh Tomar in the fifteenth century and decorated with glazed tiles in blue, yellow and green.

 

• Two things of unusual interest are found there:

 

• A temple inscription of the ninth century containing one of the oldest recorded uses of the numeral zero as a written symbol

 

• The Sas-Bahu temples and the great rock-cut Jain figures carved into the hillside

 

• The fort passed through the hands of the Tomars, the Delhi Sultans, the Mughals, the Marathas, the Scindias and the British.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gwalior is also the home of the Gwalior Gharana, the oldest gharana of khayal singing, and of Tansen, whose tomb is there and at which an annual music festival is held.

 

• Other important forts of Madhya Pradesh: Mandu, Orchha, Asirgarh and Bandhavgarh.

 

NOTE

 

• Rajasthan (Option 1): The state of the six Hill Forts inscribed by UNESCO — Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore, Amber, Jaisalmer and Gagron. It is the strongest distractor, since Rajasthan is the state most associated with forts.

 

• Maharashtra (Option 2): Known for the Maratha forts — Raigad, Sinhagad, Pratapgad, Shivneri and Torna — inscribed by UNESCO in 2025 as the *Maratha Military Landscapes*.

 

• Uttar Pradesh (Option 3): Known for the Agra Fort, the Jhansi Fort and the Fatehpur Sikri complex.

question: The COP30 United Nations Climate Change Conference, held in November 2025, took place in which country?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Brazil.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• COP30 was held at Belém, in the state of Pará, BRAZIL, in November 2025. (कॉप-30 — बेलेम, ब्राजील)

 

• The venue was chosen deliberately. Belém stands at the mouth of the Amazon, and holding the conference there placed the negotiations in the middle of the forest whose fate they concerned.

 

• The conference closed with a package to scale up climate finance, calling for the mobilisation of at least $1.3 trillion a year by 2035, and for adaptation finance to be doubled by 2025 and trebled by 2035.

 

• COP stands for Conference of the Parties to the UNFCCC, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, agreed at the Rio Earth Summit of 1992.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Recent Conferences of the Parties:

 

• COP21 (2015) – Paris; the Paris Agreement, limiting warming to well below 2°C and preferably 1.5°C

 

• COP26 (2021) – Glasgow; India announced net zero by 2070 and the Panchamrit commitments

 

• COP27 (2022) – Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt; the Loss and Damage Fund agreed

 

• COP28 (2023) – Dubai, UAE; the first Global Stocktake

 

• COP29 (2024) – Baku, Azerbaijan; the new climate finance goal

 

• COP30 (2025) – Belém, Brazil

 

• India also launched, at COP26, the LiFE initiative — Lifestyle for Environment.

 

NOTE

 

• Egypt (Option 1): Hosted COP27 at Sharm el-Sheikh in 2022.

 

• United Arab Emirates (Option 3): Hosted COP28 at Dubai in 2023.

 

• Azerbaijan (Option 4): Hosted COP29 at Baku in 2024 — the conference immediately preceding, and therefore the strongest distractor.

question: How many medals in total did India win at the Paris Olympic Games of 2024?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 6.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• India won SIX medals at the Paris Olympics of 2024 — one silver and five bronze, with no gold. India finished 71st in the medal table. (पेरिस ओलंपिक 2024 — 6 पदक)

 

• The six medallists:

 

• Manu Bhaker – bronze, 10 m air pistol; and a second bronze in the 10 m air pistol mixed team with Sarabjot Singh. She became the first Indian woman to win an Olympic shooting medal, and the first Indian since independence to win two medals at a single Games.

 

• Swapnil Kusale – bronze, 50 m rifle three positions

 

• Indian men's hockey team – bronze, retaining the medal won at Tokyo

 

• Neeraj Chopra – silver, javelin throw, having won gold at Tokyo

 

• Aman Sehrawat – bronze, men's 57 kg freestyle wrestling; at 21, the youngest Indian medallist at a Summer Olympics

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's best Olympic performance remains Tokyo 2020, with seven medals including one gold — Neeraj Chopra's javelin, India's first ever in athletics.

 

• At the Paris Paralympics 2024 India did far better, winning 29 medals — 7 gold, 9 silver and 13 bronze — its best ever.

 

NOTE

 

• 4 (Option 1): Fewer than India's actual tally, and closer to the returns of the 1990s and early 2000s.

 

• 10 (Option 2): India has never won ten medals at a single Summer Olympics.

 

• 7 (Option 3): The tally at Tokyo 2020, India's best at a Summer Olympics — and the strongest distractor here, since the two Games are constantly compared.

question: The "Great Bath", a large tank built of burnt brick and made watertight with a layer of bitumen, was found at which Harappan site?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mohenjodaro.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Great Bath was found at MOHENJODARO, in the citadel area of the city, and is the most celebrated single structure of the Harappan civilisation. (विशाल स्नानागार — मोहनजोदड़ो)

 

• It measures about 11.9 metres by 7 metres and is about 2.4 metres deep, with steps leading down at either end.

 

• Its construction shows unusual skill: the floor and walls are of finely fitted burnt brick, made watertight by a layer of bitumen between two courses, and there is an outlet at one corner for emptying it.

 

• Its purpose is believed to have been ritual bathing rather than ordinary use, since it stands within the citadel and is surrounded by a colonnade and small rooms.

 

• Mohenjodaro means "the mound of the dead" in Sindhi. It was excavated by R.D. Banerji in 1922, and lies on the Indus in the Larkana district of Sindh, in present-day Pakistan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Harappan sites and their characteristic finds:

 

• Mohenjodaro – Great Bath, Great Granary, the bronze Dancing Girl, the Priest-King, the Pashupati seal

 

• Harappa – granaries, cemetery R-37, the sandstone dancing torso

 

• Lothal – dockyard, bead factory, Persian Gulf seal

 

• Kalibangan – ploughed field, fire altars

 

• Dholavira – water reservoirs, the signboard, a stadium

 

• Rakhigarhi – the largest Harappan site in India

 

NOTE

 

• Harappa (Option 2): The site that gave the civilisation its name, excavated by Daya Ram Sahni in 1921. Its distinctive finds are the granaries and the workmen's quarters, not a bath.

 

• Dholavira (Option 3): In the Rann of Kutch, remarkable for its system of reservoirs for storing rainwater — an elaborate water arrangement, but of a quite different kind.

 

• Kalibangan (Option 4): In Rajasthan, known for the earliest ploughed field yet found and for rows of fire altars.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?

I. Insulin is a peptide hormone secreted by the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans.
II. Adrenaline is secreted by the cortex of the adrenal gland.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement I is CORRECT. Insulin is a peptide hormone secreted by the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. (इंसुलिन — बीटा कोशिकाएँ)

 

• It lowers the level of glucose in the blood, and its deficiency or ineffectiveness causes diabetes mellitus.

 

• The alpha cells of the same islets secrete glucagon, which does the opposite — it raises blood glucose.

 

• Statement II is INCORRECT. Adrenaline is secreted by the MEDULLA of the adrenal gland, not by the cortex.

 

• The adrenal medulla — the inner part — secretes adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline, the hormones of the "fight or flight" response.

 

• The adrenal cortex — the outer part — secretes a different group: cortisol, aldosterone and small quantities of sex hormones.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Adrenaline is called the "emergency hormone". It raises the heart rate and blood pressure, dilates the pupils and the air passages, and releases glucose into the blood — preparing the body for sudden exertion.

 

• Endocrine glands and their principal hormones:

 

• Pituitary – growth hormone; called the master gland

 

• Thyroid – thyroxine; its deficiency causes goitre

 

• Pancreas – insulin and glucagon

 

• Adrenal – adrenaline (medulla), cortisol (cortex)

 

• Testes – testosterone; Ovaries – oestrogen and progesterone

 

NOTE

 

• Since Statement I is correct and Statement II is not, Option 2 (Only II), Option 3 (Both I and II) and Option 4 (Neither I nor II) are all ruled out.

 

• The trap in Statement II is a correct gland with the wrong part of it. Where a statement names a structure as precisely as *cortex* or *medulla*, that precision is usually where the error has been placed.

question: Which Indian state is the largest producer of iron ore?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Odisha.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• ODISHA is the largest producer of iron ore in India, accounting for roughly half of the country's output. (ओडिशा — लौह अयस्क का सबसे बड़ा उत्पादक)

 

• Its principal deposits are in the Keonjhar, Sundargarh and Mayurbhanj districts, in the belt of the Badampahar, Gurumahisani and Sulaipat mines.

 

• The order of the producing states is Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Jharkhand.

 

• India's iron ore is of high quality, chiefly haematite (about 70% iron) and magnetite (about 72% iron, and the finest quality). The bulk of the reserves lie in a belt running through Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The four types of iron ore, in descending order of quality:

 

• Magnetite – about 72% iron; the best; magnetic

 

• Haematite – about 60-70%; the most widely used in India

 

• Limonite – about 40-60%; Siderite – about 40-50%

 

• India is among the largest producers of iron ore in the world, and exports chiefly to China and Japan through the ports of Paradip, Visakhapatnam and Mormugao.

 

• The largest steel plants are at Bhilai (Chhattisgarh), Rourkela (Odisha), Bokaro and Jamshedpur (Jharkhand) and Durgapur (West Bengal) — all sited near the ore.

 

NOTE

 

• Jharkhand (Option 1): Home of the oldest iron ore mining in India, at Noamundi and Gua, and of the Tata works at Jamshedpur. It now stands fourth in output, which makes it a genuine distractor.

 

• Chhattisgarh (Option 3): Second in output, with the great deposits of Bailadila and Dalli-Rajhara in the Bastar and Durg districts.

 

• Karnataka (Option 4): Third, with the mines of Bellary-Hospet, Kudremukh and Sandur. Kudremukh's ore is magnetite of very fine quality.

question: Pandit Hariprasad Chaurasia is a maestro of which musical instrument?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bansuri (flute).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Pandit Hariprasad Chaurasia is the foremost living exponent of the BANSURI, the Indian bamboo flute. (बांसुरी — पंडित हरिप्रसाद चौरसिया)

 

• He was born at Allahabad in 1938, the son of a wrestler who wished him to follow the same trade, and learnt music in secret.

 

• He learnt from Annapurna Devi, the daughter of Ustad Allauddin Khan, after persuading her over a long period to accept him — and, famously, learnt to play left-handed at her insistence, so as to begin afresh.

 

• With Shivkumar Sharma he composed film music under the name "Shiv-Hari", for *Silsila*, *Chandni*, *Lamhe* and *Darr*.

 

• He received the Padma Bhushan (1992) and the Padma Vibhushan (2000).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pandit Pannalal Ghosh was the first to establish the bansuri as a classical concert instrument, lengthening it to obtain the lower octaves that Hindustani music requires. Chaurasia carried the work forward.

 

• The four classes of Indian musical instrument:

 

• Sushira Vadya – wind: bansuri, shehnai, nadaswaram, pungi

 

• Tata Vadya – string: sitar, sarod, veena, santoor, sarangi

 

• Avanaddha Vadya – membrane: tabla, mridangam, pakhawaj, dhol

 

• Ghana Vadya – solid: manjira, jhanj, ghatam, morsing

 

NOTE

 

• Shehnai (Option 1): A double-reed wind instrument, and the instrument of Ustad Bismillah Khan, who received the Bharat Ratna in 2001. It is the closest distractor, being also a wind instrument of the same tradition.

 

• Nadaswaram (Option 3): The South Indian counterpart of the shehnai, and the instrument of Sheikh Chinna Moulana and T.N. Rajarathinam Pillai. It is regarded as auspicious and is played at temple ceremonies.

 

• Clarinet (Option 4): A Western instrument, taken into Carnatic music by A.K.C. Natarajan, who made it a classical concert instrument in the South.
